params.why: the car is still driving after h hours, so the time is inside the domain and some of the journey is left
the total distance D = v*T/60 is a whole number of kilometres

stem: The graph of $s(t)$ shows the distance, in $\text{km}$, that a car has travelled $t$ minutes after it set off. The graph is a straight line that starts at the origin and ends at a closed dot at the point $({=T}, {=D})$. How many kilometres of the journey does the car still have to travel after {=h} {=hword}?
solution: The closed dot shows where the journey ends. The domain is $0 \le t \le {=T}$ minutes and the range is $0 \le s \le {=D}$ km, so the whole journey is ${=D}$ km.
The time $t$ is measured in minutes, so {=h} {=hword} is $t = {=t0}$ minutes. This is inside the domain.
The graph is a straight line from the origin, so the distance travelled is proportional to the time: $s({=t0}) = \frac{{=D}}{{=T}} \times {=t0} = {=sv}$ km.
The distance still to travel is the whole journey minus the distance already travelled: ${=D} - {=sv} = {=ans}$ km.
notes:
Builds on the book's car graph (ex6-8-11a: 'What distance did the car travel in an hour?' with t in minutes, the line from the origin to the closed dot at (120, 100)). It chains the book's own unit twist (an hour is t = 60) with what the range represents (the total distance is the top of the range) and a subtraction. The graph is described in words because the engine has no figure support; the straight-line reading is done by proportion, which is what a student reads off the gridlines in the book's figure (s(60) = 50). D = v*T/60 so the speed is a whole number of km/h and s(60h) = v*h is always a whole number; remaining distance is always positive. 36 instances.
